$comment: Everything project-specific about the feature-spec gate lives here — the format rules and the workflow are project-agnostic and live in the `feature-spec` skill. Rolling the gate out to another repo means copying scripts/spec-check.mjs (+ scripts/spec-claims-reporter.mjs if a suite runs on node:test) and this file, then adjusting the paths, the layers and the commands; `scripts/install.mjs` in the skill does exactly that. Keys prefixed `$comment` are ignored by the gate and are the documentation for this file — there is no separate schema doc to keep in sync.
$comment_audience: Who the promises in this corpus are made to, in this repo's own words. NOT read by the gate — it is the declaration that settles, for whoever writes a spec, which vocabulary a promise is stated in. Free text, because the boundary sits in a different place in every product; three worked examples: `an operator on a screen: a status code or a payload key is implementation and belongs in the docs/ companion`; `an integrator calling an API: the request and its answer ARE the promise, so a refusal may name the status and the field it faults`; `a workflow author on a canvas: port names, config keys and error codes are the product's vocabulary, but the shape of a request on the wire is machinery and goes to docs/`. Whichever it is, what stays banned is the implementation behind the promise — modules, components, function names — and that half IS checked, by implementationPattern.
audience: an operator on a screen: a status code or a payload key is implementation and belongs in the docs/ companion
$comment_ticketPattern: Shape of a ticket id in this project's tracker. Optional — drop the key and every ticket reference goes unchecked. `AC-<n>` is reserved for acceptance-criterion ids and is never read as a ticket, so a tracker whose team key is literally `AC` cannot be checked here.
$comment_implementationPattern: What counts as naming the implementation in a spec. A promise that names a component or a module rots silently on the first rename — nothing goes red, which is why the ban is checked rather than advised. `.md` stays legal so specs can link each other, and sibling links get their own existence check. Optional: drop the key and this TypeScript-shaped default applies. The trailing lookahead is not decoration: without it `.js` matches inside `.json`, so a spec naming a published `.well-known/…json` document is reported for naming the implementation. A repository on another stack sets its own here rather than editing the script — e.g. add `|\bapp/\S+|\b[\w./-]+\.(?:php|py|go)` for those stacks.
$comment_companions: Files in the spec directory that are not specs — a glossary, a conventions note. They carry no acceptance criteria, so without this key the gate would report one as a spec missing its frontmatter, its introduction and its `## Tickets`. `README.md` is exempt separately, because it is the index and has checks of its own.
$comment_houseRules: Where this repository's own additions to the format are written down — what counts as a surface here, the cuts already made, the words this corpus settled, a title convention, a vocabulary boundary finer than `audience` can state. `README.md` is the default because the index is where three of those already belong and it is exempt from the spec checks in its own right; any other file in the spec directory works too — its bare filename, the way `companions` and a sibling link name one — but then name it in `companions` as well, or it is reported as a spec missing its frontmatter. Read it before writing or revising a spec. NOT read by the gate. Two limits, or it becomes a loophole: it may narrow and extend what the skill says but never switch off a rule the gate checks (widening the implementation ban is `implementationPattern`, not a sentence beside it), and nothing that already has a key here belongs in it — `suites`, `ceiling`, `audience`, `ticketPattern`, `indexRegister` are settled in this file, and stating them twice produces two truths about one thing. Optional: drop the key in a repo that keeps nothing of its own.
$comment_indexRegister: Heading of the section in the index that records surfaces carrying no promise yet. Each row names the ticket that will promise its surface, so a ticket named there must not already be history in a spec's `## Tickets` — that would mean the promise landed and the row outlived it. Optional: drop the key and the register goes unchecked.
$comment_indexAsides: The index's other non-inventory sections, by heading. The inventory check reads the index as “everything except these and `indexRegister`”, because a spec's entry has to be an entry of its own — and every section named here cites specs by link, so without the subtraction a bullet in one of them counts as a spec's inventory row and lets the real row be deleted in silence. The default is the four sections the skill's index table names beside the inventory and the register, which is also what `install.mjs` seeds, so a fresh repo needs no edit. Rename one of those headings and this list has to come along: a heading that is not found is skipped, which reads that section as inventory again — the behaviour before this key existed rather than a new failure, and the reason an entry in those sections opens on bold text or a name rather than on a link. The inventory cannot be named positively instead: a corpus of any size groups its inventory under headings of its own and adds to them, so that list would go stale on the next group and take the check with it. Optional — drop the key and the whole file except the register is the inventory. An older vendored `spec-check.mjs` ignores it rather than failing on it.
indexAsides: How a spec is cut here
The surfaces, and what the product calls them
$comment_formDebt: One rule of the written form, held by a ratchet rather than a plain check: a `## Gaps` entry sits under one of three bold labels (`Undecided` / `Known` / `Unreachable`). The figure must match what the corpus actually contains, in both directions — adding a violation fails, and so does fixing one without lowering the number here, which is what keeps the figure equal to reality rather than to whenever somebody last looked. A fresh corpus starts at 0, so the ratchet acts as an outright gate; a corpus that predates the rule starts at whatever it contains and works down. What a ratchet cannot see is a swap — fix one violation and add another and the total is unchanged — so it is a floor under new writing, not a guarantee about any one file. Drop the key and the labels go unchecked, along with the reserved meaning of a bold line inside `## Gaps`.
$comment_ceiling: What the test harness here cannot reach at any layer — the rule that routes a promise out of the ordered layers and into `manual` or `todo`. NOT read by the gate, and NOT a definition of what a layer means: `unit`, `feature` and `e2e` mean the same thing in every repository (the skill names the order), while the ceiling is genuinely local. A library that mocks its FTP, SMTP and storage transports writes it as: a criterion about the file actually arriving is `manual` with a reason, or `todo` with a ticket — never `unit`. Optional: drop the key in a repo whose harness can reach everything it promises.
$comment_suites: Which of the ordered layers this repository has, and how to enumerate each one. The gate reads the names from this file — its vocabulary is these keys plus `manual` and `todo`, so a `verify:` line naming a layer absent here is a hard error. Declare only the layers that exist: a repo with two is not deficient, and a promise no declared layer can prove says `manual` or `todo` instead. Never add a layer to make a `verify:` line legal — two suites listing the same tests are not two layers, and every claim then arrives twice. `runHint` is not read by the gate either; it is the command for whoever has to run one feature's proofs by hand.
$comment_adapters: `adapter` names the listing parser, and there are four. `playwright` reads `playwright test --list --reporter=json` and takes claims from real tags. `vitest` reads a flat `[{ name, file }]` array and takes claims from the test title — where such a suite is narrowed to a directory, the flag goes LAST, `vitest list <dir> --json`, because `--json` takes an optional value and reads a directory that follows it as the file to write the listing into, which fails on EISDIR; `vitest list --dir <dir> --json` is a third form and the silent one, exiting 0 with an empty listing. `phpunit` reads `--list-tests-xml=php://stdout` and takes claims from the `<groups>` block, so a PHP test claims with `#[Group('spec:feature:AC-n')]` — add the bare `#[Group('spec:feature')]` too, which is inert to the gate and is what makes `--group spec:<feature>` a usable filter. `go` reads the `attr` events of `go test -json` and takes claims from `t.Attr("spec", "feature:AC-n")` (Go 1.25+) — real tag support, and the `spec:` prefix is optional in the value because the key already carries it. It reads a RUN rather than a listing, because `go test -list` prints top-level function names and nothing else: no subtests, no attributes. Two consequences. A failing claiming test takes the listing down and coverage reads as unknown rather than absent; and a suite needing a live stack can only be enumerated with that stack UP and green, which is why such a repo runs the gate inside the job that already brings the stack up rather than in one of its own. The test cache is NOT a hazard — measured on go1.27, a cached package replays its attributes, and editing a test invalidates its package, so `-count=1` on a command is about a live stack and never about the adapter. Unlike `vitest` and `phpunit`, a Go skip IS visible: the test's terminal action is `skip` and it arrives after the attribute. node:test has no listing mode, so it borrows the `vitest` adapter via the bundled reporter, which runs only the claiming tests and prints that same array — `node --test --test-reporter=./scripts/spec-claims-reporter.mjs --test-name-pattern='@spec:' '<dir>/**/*.test.*'` — the glob has to be quoted, because a bare directory is read as a file name and the run fails before collecting anything. Two consequences of running rather than listing: only the tests that carry a claim run at all, and a claiming test that FAILS takes the suite's listing down with it, so the gate reports coverage as unknown until the proof of that promise is green again. Any runner that can print `[{ name, file }]` needs no new adapter either. One blind spot per adapter, worth knowing before trusting a green run: `playwright` sees a static `test.skip` and rejects it, `vitest` listings omit skipped tests so they arrive as 'nothing claims this', and `phpunit`'s listing is static while its skips are runtime, so a `markTestSkipped` is invisible here. `go` has no blind spot of this kind and a different cost instead — it pays for a test run to enumerate.
$comment_fileset: `fileset` is optional and only means something when two suites share it: they enumerate the SAME test files and differ in the tier they run in — the same UI files with the backend mocked in the pull-request gate, and against the real stack nightly. A claim then arrives from both listings, and the gate treats a claim from a sibling tier as legitimate extra proof rather than a mismatched level. What still has to hold is that the tier an AC names carries a claim of its own, which is how a test filtered out of the mocked tier (Playwright's `@real-only` and the like) forces the promise to say `smoke` rather than `e2e`. This does not reorder the layers: both tiers sit at the same rung and answer one question between them — is this promise gated on the way in? Leave `fileset` out where each suite has files of its own.
$comment_container: Where a listing runs. Nothing declared means on this host, in the repo root or in `nativeCwd`. A suite that names a `container` (with the optional `workdir`, and the top-level `compose` file) has its command wrapped in `docker compose exec -T`, which is what a repository whose toolchain lives only in its dev stack needs — no container mounts the docker socket, so nothing inside one can reach a sibling. `--native` forces every suite onto the host and is for CI, which installs the toolchains directly and has no stack to exec into; a suite with no `container` is unaffected by the flag either way.
